question.text: How are debt and money market instruments typically valued for NAV computation in a mutual fund scheme?

answer.text: Under SEBI/AMFI valuation guidelines based on fair valuation principles, using current market/fair value inputs as applicable
Always at their face value until maturity
At the purchase price paid by the mutual fund
At the last traded price on the stock exchange only

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the NISM Series V-A workbook (pp.40, 138, 143), debt and money-market instruments held in mutual fund schemes are valued under SEBI/AMFI valuation guidelines, applying fair-valuation principles and using current market/fair-value inputs as applicable. The aim is a true and fair NAV that reflects current market conditions and yields. The Trap: Face value ignores the impact of interest-rate and credit changes on bond prices. Purchase price (historical cost) does not reflect current market conditions. "Last traded price only" is insufficient because many debt securities trade infrequently — fair-valuation inputs are needed even when there is no recent traded price. Note: Explain to clients that debt funds are not fixed-deposit substitutes — their NAV can fluctuate due to fair-value/mark-to-market movements in the underlying portfolio. Duration and credit quality matter when selecting a debt fund and should be matched to the investor's horizon.
